reports.title: Distributed split computing using diffusive metrics for UAV swarms

identity.excerpt: Distributed split computing using diffusive metrics for UAV swarms

architecture.finding: Swarm nodes exchange local capacity metrics with one-hop neighbors; repeated exchanges propagate workload information beyond one hop. There is no global scheduler in the proposed method.

workload.finding: The simulator processes a modeled layered inference graph with two intermediate exits. The evaluation identifies an application example, with no named input dataset or specified neural-network implementation.

partition_assignment.finding: A node can forward raw inputs or already computed intermediate state to a neighbor, choosing a layer exit depth with respect to load. The method bounds redundant reconsideration.

optimization.finding: The algorithm combines a diffused compute-capacity indicator, a threshold on offloading, and a congestion-aware early exit. Sensitivity to the threshold is evaluated separately.

compute_radio.finding: Compute capacity is parameterized across heterogeneous UAVs. The two-ray channel and transmission rate are modeled. Table 2 gives simulator settings rather than hardware validation.

mobility_continuity.finding: Circular UAV trajectories and mostly line-of-sight connections drive modeled neighbor changes. Constraint and queue behavior mitigates redistribution loops. Physical node failure and recovery are not evaluated in the inspected simulation.

evaluation.finding: The evaluation is software simulation with stochastic arrivals, mobility and heterogeneous nodes. It describes repeated independent runs, with no physical UAV test in the evaluation.

baselines.finding: Comparisons include random and acyclic-random offloading, a least-busy greedy scheme and local-only inference. The proposed distributed method is the fifth case.

outcomes.finding: The evaluation reports latency, outstanding work, transfer time, energy per task and fairness under scenario sweeps. Interpret early-exit results in the context of the model’s assumed exit accuracies.

variability.finding: Section 5 reports 95% intervals derived from 50 independent runs and varies threshold, worker count and task intensity, among other inputs.

code_data.finding: No simulator/code release or application dataset is specified in the inspected simulation, conclusion and acknowledgment.

funding_conflicts.finding: The Acknowledgment names ITU and PRIN 2022 support. The inspected first page and end matter do not contain a competing-interest declaration.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 12, first page and Acknowledgment

limitations.finding: The authors call for advanced mobility models and real-flight data and identify field-operation needs in runtime monitoring, parameter tuning and early-exit accuracy policy.

reports.title: Edge-Cloud Collaborative Model Inference for Aerial Networks with Distributionally Diverse Data

identity.excerpt: Edge-Cloud Collaborative Model Inference for Aerial Networks with Distributionally Diverse Data

architecture.finding: Multiple aerial edge nodes independently extract features and collaborate with one ground/cloud server via a modeled radio access network.

workload.finding: CIFAR-10 test images are augmented to synthesize non-identical data across UAVs. ResNet-18/34 act as edge backbones and ResNet-101/152 act as cloud backbones.

partition_assignment.finding: Cloud processing of uploaded features estimates confidence, then a per-UAV threshold selects cases requiring an additional quantized raw upload.

optimization.finding: The study uses per-UAV thresholds and raw-data quantization for accuracy maximization within a shared bandwidth limit, with alternating optimization.

compute_radio.finding: The setup names a cloud GPU and models per-UAV spectral efficiency and bandwidth. The 100 Mbps value applies to the Table I comparison. No flight radio or onboard hardware characterization is given there.

mobility_continuity.finding: No UAV trajectory, outage or recovery evaluation is reported in the configuration or results. Spectral efficiency differences do not establish mobility validation.

evaluation.finding: The edge–cloud experiment is simulated using synthesized data distributions. The cloud processing hardware is identified; there is no demonstrated flight test in this experiment.

baselines.finding: Raw-Only sends raw data, Feat-Only sends extracted features, and GSUP uses shared confidence/quantization settings. Table I compares them with the proposed policy.

outcomes.finding: The proposed policy reports higher top-1 accuracy across Table I model pairs and lower simulated end-to-end latency than Raw-Only. Its point-estimate latency is higher than GSUP and Feat-Only.

variability.finding: The paper reports three independent seeds per setting and 95% Student-t confidence intervals. Fig. 2 is a single-UAV bandwidth and confidence-threshold sweep; Fig. 3 varies UAV count.

code_data.finding: The underlying CIFAR-10 data are named and cited. No study-specific source code, generated input splits or simulation artifacts are identified in the inspected setup and end matter.

funding_conflicts.finding: The acknowledgment names multiple funding programs. The first page and end matter inspected do not contain a competing-interest declaration.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 6, first page and Acknowledgement

limitations.finding: The results describe a latency cost for deeper cloud backbones and a smaller accuracy gain where upstream information is limited. The conclusion does not provide a dedicated limitations discussion.

reports.title: Aeroagrinet: Swarm-Enabled Flying Edge Framework for Real-Time Agricultural Intelligence

identity.excerpt: Aeroagrinet: Swarm-Enabled Flying Edge Framework for Real-Time Agricultural Intelligence

architecture.finding: A layered flying-edge system uses coordinated UAVs with onboard inference, ground sensor connections and optional cloud synchronization.

workload.finding: The paper describes crop-pest detection, vegetation and soil monitoring, and yield prediction. It reports lightweight CNN edge benchmarking, but does not identify specific input datasets for those benchmarks.

partition_assignment.finding: Onboard inference tasks are assigned or reassigned across drones. The cited design is task-level allocation with local inference; no layer-level split is described in the relevant sections.

optimization.finding: Coverage coordination and energy-aware task allocation support the design, alongside a redundancy and consensus policy. A reproducible mathematical allocation objective is not given in the inspected architecture sections.

compute_radio.finding: The field-prototype description identifies camera/sensor connections, Raspberry Pi and Coral devices, LoRaWAN-connected IoT sensors and ROS coordination. Hardware descriptions are distinct from unreported radio parameters.

mobility_continuity.finding: The design describes self-healing connectivity and redundant reassignment. Dropout and packet-loss results are reported, with no explicit link assigning the individual dropout comparison to the hardware field prototype.
mobility_continuity.original_locator: pp. 3 and 5–6, §§II.D, III.B, V.F and V.K

evaluation.finding: The authors describe simulation with NS-3, ROS, Gazebo and MATLAB UAV Toolbox and a separate author-reported DJI/Raspberry Pi/Coral field prototype.

baselines.finding: The paper identifies two comparator classes: conventional centrally tasked UAVs and cloud-based monitoring. Detailed reproduction of comparator hardware and network parity is not established by that summary.

outcomes.finding: Reported measures include decision and inference latency, energy and completion under load or dropout. Simulated and emulated conditions are explicitly named for some measures; modality is not assigned figure-by-figure.

variability.finding: The paper varies coordinated swarm load and dropout conditions. The text and comparison figures inspected do not establish independent repeat counts or uncertainty intervals.

code_data.finding: The simulation tools and prototype components are named, but no study code, data or artifact release is given at the inspected locations.

funding_conflicts.finding: The inspected first page and end sections lack study funding and competing-interest statements.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 6, first page, conclusion and end matter

limitations.finding: The discussion and conclusion describe intended benefits without an explicit limitations or threats-to-validity statement.

reports.title: A DRL-Assisted Decentralized Framework for UAV Swarm Collaborative Inference

identity.excerpt: A DRL-Assisted Decentralized Framework for UAV Swarm Collaborative Inference

architecture.finding: The simulated swarm is decentralized, with two UAVs collaborating per inference. The task pipeline is distinct from swarm population; Table IV gives the default and Table X varies it.
architecture.original_locator: pp. 5–6, 10–11 and 15, §III.E and Tables IV and X

workload.finding: The workload uses image minibatches and profiled model configurations, including four networks in Table V and an additional transfer-analysis model. Named source image data are not reported in the setup.

partition_assignment.finding: Each task can pair its source with a selected neighbor and split a DNN at a candidate layer. The mini-batch pipeline overlaps communication and processing, with a local option.

optimization.finding: The model uses a Pareto shortlist and DQN to jointly select the partner and partition under variable neighborhood availability and deadline/energy trade-offs.

compute_radio.finding: The hardware-grounded model represents heterogeneous Jetson-class compute and Wi-Fi 802.11ac airborne links. These radio and compute settings are simulator parameters.

mobility_continuity.finding: The simulator models changing neighbors and link interruptions. The design includes assignment or local fallback handling. This is software evaluation rather than field-validated recovery.

evaluation.finding: A custom Gymnasium simulator and a PyTorch/Stable-Baselines3 learner evaluate a set of common-seed episodes. Named hardware characteristics inform simulated compute profiles.

baselines.finding: Collaborative heuristics are tested on a shared two-UAV pipeline, and Local is a separate noncollaborative comparator. Table V distinguishes original EPCTA from its same-substrate adaptation.

outcomes.finding: Under VGG-16 and VGG-19, the proposed method reports higher deadline satisfaction than the strongest same-substrate comparator. Local remains competitive on lighter workloads. Latency in Table V is end-to-end P50.

variability.finding: Training is assessed over three seeds and main evaluation over 30 independent episodes. The evaluation reports uncertainty, paired significance tests and sensitivity and ablation results.

code_data.finding: The reproducibility paragraph reports source code, environment, baselines and entry points at github.com/cupofcup/DDCI and gives training/test seed settings.

funding_conflicts.finding: The first page declares funding. The inspected first page and end matter do not contain a competing-interest statement.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 15–16, funding footnote and end matter

limitations.finding: The article explicitly excludes propulsion power and detailed MAC effects and calls for extending energy modeling to battery balancing. A fully matched DRL backbone study is deferred.

quantitative_rows.denominator: strict all-arrived-tasks; mean ± SD over 30 common-seed episodes
quantitative_rows.workload: VGG-16 in the custom Gymnasium simulator
quantitative_rows.conditions: shared two-UAV mini-batch substrate, different decision policies; result applies to this workload and comparator
quantitative_rows.locator: Table V, VGG-16, DDCI (Ours) and Comm-Min rows, Deadline Sat. (%)

reports.title: Robust Group Target Awareness Inference in Multi-UAV-Enabled ISCC Networks Based on Split Deep Reinforcement Learning

identity.excerpt: Robust Group Target Awareness Inference in Multi-UAV-Enabled ISCC Networks Based on Split Deep Reinforcement Learning

architecture.finding: A multi-UAV system coordinates compute among airborne nodes and distributes inference within the airborne group.

workload.finding: The evaluation uses a layered neural network and software workload profiles. No underlying input dataset is identified in the inspected setup.

partition_assignment.finding: The architecture allocates sequential portions of a split neural workload across participating UAVs.

optimization.finding: The study evaluates a learning-based coordination method with centralized training and decentralized execution.

compute_radio.finding: The system defines compute and radio models and specifies simulator configurations, distinct from measured airborne deployment.

mobility_continuity.finding: The software evaluation varies node participation and inspects the ability to continue inference after node losses. Hardware recovery is not demonstrated.

evaluation.finding: The authors report Python/PyTorch numerical simulation with a GPU for the study configuration. The evaluation is not a live or hardware testbed study.

baselines.finding: The evaluation compares alternative partition policies, learning methods, and component variants.

outcomes.finding: The simulation reports task completion and inference-quality measures under alternative conditions. The findings are limited to the described software experiments.

variability.finding: The evaluation varies study conditions and reports convergence. The inspected results do not state independent trial counts, seeds or outcome uncertainty.

code_data.finding: No study-specific software, traces or input dataset availability statement is identified in the inspected simulation setup, discussion and end matter.

funding_conflicts.finding: The funding footnote identifies national and regional grant support. No competing-interest statement is given in the inspected first page and end matter.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 14–15, funding footnote and end matter

limitations.finding: The discussion reports constraints on transferring a trained policy beyond its configured size. The conclusion identifies topics left to future work, including energy and privacy.

reports.title: Joint Semantic Compression and Resource Allocation for Multi-UAV Networks: A Knowledge-Guided Reinforcement Learning Approach

identity.excerpt: Joint Semantic Compression and Resource Allocation for Multi-UAV Networks: A Knowledge-Guided Reinforcement Learning Approach

architecture.finding: Multiple UAV semantic experts process observations from different views. A coordinating UAV fuses representations and sends a task-oriented description over a modeled downlink.

workload.finding: The study tests COCO-based visual question answering, identifies multiple edge expert backbones, and uses a task-specific semantic representation and codec.

partition_assignment.finding: Inference uses distributed per-UAV representation extraction and task-guided collaborative fusion, with selectable semantic symbol granularity.

optimization.finding: A two-stage learner jointly adjusts the UAV contribution weights and representation granularity toward task quality under a communication constraint.

compute_radio.finding: The setup gives a Jetson-class onboard compute profile, modeled channels and a workstation for the PyTorch implementation. The compatibility profile is distinct from on-device flight validation.

mobility_continuity.finding: The channel varies in the simulation. No explicit UAV trajectory, loss-based reassignment or recovery evaluation is reported in the inspected methods and results.

evaluation.finding: Simulation on an RTX workstation evaluates collaborative VQA under modeled communication settings. Table II characterizes candidate experts relative to onboard resources.

baselines.finding: The evaluation compares policy learning against PPO and other control variants, then evaluates fusion against expert alternatives and the task-specific best single expert.

outcomes.finding: The study reports learning, task quality, granularity control and per-task accuracy. Comparisons against a single expert and controller ablations answer different questions.

variability.finding: The study varies SNR, semantic granularity, task type and training parameters. The inspected evaluation does not establish independent repeat counts or run-level outcome intervals.

code_data.finding: A COCO-based VQA dataset is named. There is no release route for study code, generated input configurations or simulation scripts in the inspected sections.

funding_conflicts.finding: The first page and final pre-reference text do not state study funding or competing interests.

limitations.finding: The authors identify inter-UAV exchange overhead, synchronization under heterogeneous delays and onboard real-time implementation as open deployment issues.

reports.title: RDI-LLM: A Resilient Distributed Inference Framework for LLMs in Resource-Constrained UAV Swarms

identity.excerpt: RDI-LLM: A Resilient Distributed Inference Framework for LLMs in Resource-Constrained UAV Swarms

architecture.finding: An ad hoc swarm uses a leader to coordinate transformer inference among UAV workers with redundant shards.

workload.finding: The simulator supports two FP16 Llama-2 sizes. Main displayed results use the 70B workload. The setup does not identify an empirical task or prompt dataset.

partition_assignment.finding: The method deploys redundant feed-forward shards offline and activates worker replicas selectively online. Leader-side state and worker-side aggregation have different roles.

optimization.finding: The optimization uses an offline placement phase and an online solver coordinating selective execution and communication under resource and reliability constraints.

compute_radio.finding: The simulator uses parameterized compute and 3GPP-informed channel assumptions. Table III separates propagation parameters and study-specific operating settings.

mobility_continuity.finding: Worker redundancy, leader re-election and checkpoint recovery are described. Stress tests vary simulated network and mobility conditions. The paper leaves real-hardware recovery latency unmeasured.

evaluation.finding: A discrete-event simulator tests fixed and stress conditions, with independent seeds and a shared timeout. The article explicitly leaves the physical prototype and on-device solver timing for future work.

baselines.finding: The evaluation uses parallelism, partition/deployment, random and alternative scheduling baselines, with separate component ablations. Shared conditions and baseline adaptations are documented.

outcomes.finding: The reported outcomes include completion, energy and latency. In the default 70B simulated comparison, latency is conditioned on success; reliability and latency therefore require separate interpretation.

variability.finding: The study gives independent-seed counts for default and stress settings and tests model parameters, mobility and channel scenarios separately.

code_data.finding: The simulator design and model family are named. No study-specific repository, trace release or input dataset is identified in the inspected evaluation and end matter.

funding_conflicts.finding: The footnote discloses government and university support. The inspected first page and final sections do not give a competing-interest statement.
funding_conflicts.original_locator: pp. 1 and 14–15, funding footnote and end matter

limitations.finding: The paper describes the redundancy–memory and deployment cost trade-off, interference-related limits and lack of validation of leader operation on real UAVs.
